title: Principles of confounder selection - Tyler J VanderWeele
text:
Confounding by covariates C of the relationship between exposure A and outcome Y


The article “Principles of Confounder Selection”, by Tyler J. VanderWeele, published in the European Journal of Epidemiology in 2019 (PMCID: PMC6447501 PMID: 30840181), highlights the importance of correctly selecting confounding factors in observational studies to make valid causal inferences. VanderWeele proposes a practical approach based on identifying variables that are causes of the exposure, the outcome, or both, and suggests excluding those that act as instrumental variables. He also considers the inclusion of proxies for unmeasured variables that may be common causes. The article seeks to balance the need to control confounding factors while avoiding the introduction of additional biases, especially in contexts where the causal structure is not fully understood.
Additionally, statistical strategies for selecting covariates in causal studies are discussed, including traditional methods such as forward/backward selection and changes in estimation, as well as more recent approaches like HDPS (High-Dimensional Propensity Scores) and machine learning techniques. It is emphasised that, despite methodological advances, substantive knowledge remains crucial for good selection.
From my experience, this article was a real gateway into the world of causal inference. I found it valuable not only for its conceptual clarity but also because VanderWeele effectively tackles a complex issue with well-grounded and practical recommendations. I consider it essential reading for those starting to face the challenge of controlling for confounding in observational studies, and a reference I return to frequently. Without a doubt, it is one of those works that leaves a lasting impact on anyone interested in causality.

title: Curriculum Vitae
text:
🔬 Research Interests
My research interests lie in understanding complex population processes — particularly within public health — through the lens of mathematical and statistical modelling. I am especially interested in how stochastic and longitudinal frameworks can capture dynamic, latent, and time-dependent phenomena in health and demographic data, and how these tools can inform evidence-based public health decision-making.
Statistical Interests:

Stochastic Processes (Markov chains, latent Markov models, stochastic differential equations)
Bayesian Statistics
Longitudinal and Multilevel Models
Statistical and Machine Learning
Causal Inference

Areas of Application:

Epidemiology and Demography: Mortality, Migration, Fertility, and Population Dynamics
Non-communicable Diseases and Mental Health: Risk trajectories, comorbidities, and psychosocial determinants
Substance Use: Transitions and progression patterns among youth populations
Infectious Disease Modelling: Transmission dynamics and the impact of behavioural interventions
Health Inequities and Environmental Health: Socioeconomic and geographic determinants of health outcomes
